segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If I speak in the tongues of humans and of angels but do not have love, I have become resounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if I have the gift of prophecy and know all the secrets and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if I give away all I own to feed others, and if I hand over my body so that I may be burned, but do not have love, I gain nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Love is patient; love is kind. Love does not envy; it does not brag, is not puffed up,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: does not behave shamefully, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked to anger, keeps no account of wrongs,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: does not rejoice at injustice, but rejoices with the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Love never fails. But as for prophecies, they will be done away with; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will be done away with.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we know in part and we prophesy in part;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but when what is complete comes, what is in part will be done away with.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I did away with the ways of a child.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For now we see in a mirror, as in a riddle, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, just as I too have been fully known.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And now faith, hope, love remain—these three; and the greatest of these is love.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a language as well as for the organ of speech. “Tongues” is kept here because it is the established English name for the gift of inspired speech that Paul discusses throughout chapters 12–14, but a first-century reader would have heard simply “the languages of humans and of angels.”

The Greek says only “bronze that makes a noise.” Most versions take this to be a gong; some scholars think instead of the bronze vessels used to amplify sound in theaters. Either way the image is of an object that produces sound without meaning.

In Jewish Greek of the period this word is the ordinary term for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. English “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, which is not the point. Most English versions keep “mysteries” as an established technical term, and many scholars defend that practice.

notes.phrase: so that I may be burned
notes.note: The manuscripts are divided between two verbs that differ by a single letter in Greek. The SBLGNT, followed here, reads “so that I may be burned.” Several of the earliest manuscripts read “so that I may boast,” which the standard critical editions and a number of recent translations adopt. The question remains disputed.

notes.traditional: thinketh no evil; is not resentful; keeps no record of wrongs
notes.note: The verb is a bookkeeping term meaning to reckon or enter in an account, and the object is literally “the evil.” The rendering takes this as not keeping a tally of injuries received, which is the majority view today. The phrase can also mean “does not plan evil,” as the older English versions understood it.

The verb can mean either “bear, put up with” or “cover, protect,” and both senses are attested in the period. Paul’s other uses (1 Corinthians 9:12; 1 Thessalonians 3:1, 5) favor “bear,” but “covers all things,” meaning love shields others or keeps silent about their faults, is a serious alternative. The repeated “all things” can also be read adverbially, “always” or “in everything.”

Paul uses the same verb four times in verses 8–11, of prophecies, knowledge, the partial, and the ways of a child. It means to put something out of operation or bring it to an end. Many versions vary the English (“pass away,” “come to an end,” “give up”); one rendering is kept here so the repetition can be heard.

notes.traditional: the perfect; that which is perfect
notes.note: The word means whole, full-grown or having reached its goal, and here it stands in direct contrast with “what is in part.” “Complete” keeps that contrast, where “perfect” might suggest moral flawlessness. The traditional rendering is “the perfect,” though several modern versions also have “the complete” or “completeness.”

The Greek says “in a riddle,” that is, in an indirect or puzzling form. The wording echoes Numbers 12:8 in the Greek Old Testament, where God speaks with Moses “mouth to mouth” and “not in riddles.” The traditional “dimly” or “darkly” suggests a poor reflection, but the point is more likely that a mirror gives only an indirect view compared with seeing face to face. Ancient mirrors were of polished metal.

The phrase can be temporal (“at the present time”) or logical (“as things stand”). On the first reading faith, hope and love remain during the present age; on the second all three endure, in contrast with the gifts that will be done away with. Interpreters are divided. “Greatest” renders a Greek comparative, “greater,” which commonly served for the superlative in this period.

candidates.reason: The choice between “tongues” and “languages” for the spiritual gift must be uniform across 1 Corinthians 12–14, Acts 2, 10 and 19, and Mark 16.
The same verb is positive in 12:31 and 14:1 (“eagerly desire”) and negative here; translators vary between “envy,” “be jealous” and “be zealous,” and the link should be handled consistently.
A thematic word in 1 Corinthians (4:6, 4:18–19, 5:2, 8:1, 13:4) and Colossians 2:18, rendered variously as “puffed up,” “arrogant” or “proud”; the thread is lost if the English varies.
Recurs across Matthew, Paul, Hebrews and James, where “perfect,” “mature” and “complete” are all in use and “perfect” often misleads.
Versions vary between “unrighteousness,” “wrongdoing,” “injustice” and “iniquity,” and the rendering should be coordinated with the δίκαιος word group across the New Testament.

warnings: Verse 11: καταργέω is not rendered with a register form (nullify; abolish; bring to nothing; do away with; set aside; render powerless; release / sever; use up) and has no register-exception note.
